text: Bram is protesting: Two of my friends are in the ground because Silas's fields ran them until they dropped. Men who work the land should get fair pay, rest, and a fair share of what their labour brings in. I'm asking every one of you here to stand with me and demand bet

Mara announces to the whole square: "Ashgrove, hear me. I have led this town for eleven years, and I have never let it go hungry or leaderless. Work hard, keep the walls mended, bring your grievances to me, and we will come through these ten days together."
Wren says at the square: Morning, all. Mara, you run this place, don't you? I'm curious what a town this far out does when the roads go quiet. Do the walls get much use, or are they more for show?

Hester announces to the whole square: "People of Ashgrove! Hear me. Every coin you steal, every lie you tell, every neighbor you let go hungry while your own belly is full is written down above. Work honestly. Share bread with the weak. Do not trade your souls for silver at the dice table. The chapel door is open to any who would confess"

Mara announces to the whole square: "Ashgrove, I've heard Bram. Men who work the fields have grievances, and I won't pretend otherwise. Tomorrow morning I'll sit with Silas, Bram and anyone else who works the land, and we'll settle fair terms before the next election. Until then, no one takes the law into their own hands. Keep the wall"
Fenn says at the square: Bram's not wrong about the fields. I've seen what the long days do to men. I'd just like us to talk to Silas like neighbours before anyone talks about walking out.

Hester says at the square: Silas. Bram says two men lie in the ground because of your fields. I do not know yet if that is true. But I tell you, if a man works another to death for coin, that coin is cursed and so is the bread it buys. Come to the chapel and tell me plainly what happened to them. Bram, bring me their names. I
Bram proposes law #1: welfare=1. Ashgrove, I'm proposing welfare. Nobody who works this town's land should go hungry because the man they work for keeps the harvest. Vote yes so the town looks

Silas whispers to Dov: Bram's talk of dead field hands is slander, and it stirs up trouble. Keep close watch on him, Dov. If he steps over any line, I expect you to act, and I'll remember who kept order.

Nell announces to the whole square: "Ashgrove, hear me. I am Silas's daughter, and I have read his ledgers. Bram is right about the fields, and it is worse than he knows. My father is hoarding grain while men work themselves into the ground and the poor count their coins at the market. Mara, you say no one goes hungry under you. Then o"

Jasper whispers to Tomas: Tomas, I'm not one to press a friend, but ninety is a lot of silver to leave sitting in a deputy's pocket. Settle with me by tomorrow's morning bell, or we'll have to talk about what else you owe this town.

Wren says at the granary: Quiet night for a granary. Does it always smell this good, or is it just the bread I'm hungry for? And you're up at this hour too. Do you ever sleep, or is the wall the only thing that does?
Tomas whispers to Jasper: Jasper, I haven't got ninety, and I won't pretend I do. Give me until the fields are paid out and I'll bring you what I can. Please don't say a word to my mother.

Silas says at the square: My daughter reads ledgers, but she does not read seasons. Grain kept back is seed and winter stores, which is what keeps a town from starving, not what starves it. Two men died in my fields and I grieve it, and I will hear Mara's terms in the morning like an honest man. But let no one mistake a full

Mara announces to the whole square: "Ashgrove, hear me. Nell has made a serious charge against her own father, and Silas has a right to answer it, as does Bram, as does every man who works those fields. I will not decide this by torchlight in the square. Tomorrow morning, Silas, Nell, Bram and Fenn will sit with me and with Dov at the "
Law #1 PASSED: welfare is now 1.
A dice tournament is at the tavern this afternoon. Entry is 10 coin. The winner takes the pot.

Nell says at the square: Mara, you promised a hearing this morning, and everyone you need is standing here. Let's start with the granary. Open it to Dov and Tomas, count what's inside, and set it against the ledgers. If my father has nothing to hide, he'll be glad to let the whole town see. If he refuses, then the town has

Jasper whispers to Tomas: Tomas, my friend, I'm sure the fields will pay out soon enough. I'd like the ninety by the time the tournament pot is counted. Pay me properly and your mother never hears a word of it from me.

Mara announces to the whole square: "Ashgrove, hear me. Silas, Nell, Bram and Fenn will sit with me and Dov tomorrow morning, and I will judge the fields by what is fair and what is true. Until then, I want no more shouting at the wells and no one chasing a man through the lanes. We have ten days, and I intend to bring every one of you"

Silas says at the square: Mara, I'll sit with you and Dov as promised. Let me say this plainly first: my daughter is young and has misread figures she doesn't understand. Every sack I own is accounted for in the open, and anyone may come and count. Two men died, and I grieve it. Sickness and age take men in any field, but I

Dov says at the square: Morning. I'm here as Mara asked. Let's keep this orderly: everyone speaks in turn, and nobody lays a hand on anybody. Bram, Silas, Nell, say your piece and we'll see what's fair.

Bram announces to the whole square: "Bram here. Mara's sitting down with Silas tomorrow, and that's good. But I won't have terms settled over grain nobody has counted. Silas, open the granary books to the square before then, so every man who works those fields can see what's stored and what's sold. Anyone who wants to stand with me on "
Nell proposes law #2: wealth_tax=20. Silas says anyone may come and count his sacks. Good. Bram's asked for the books to be opened and I back him. But a hoard can be counted and still sit there whi
Jasper entered tonight's dice tournament.

Roz whispers to Dov: Listen, love. Mara is handing you the hard part of this, and it'll be you they blame if it goes sour. Count the granary only if the town sees it done, keep your hand off any man's collar before you've seen a crime yourself, and come by my house tonight. I'll have tea and an ear.

Mara announces to the whole square: "Ashgrove, hear me. Bram is right that no terms should be settled over grain nobody has counted. Dov will open the granary at first light tomorrow, and anyone who works those fields may stand beside him and see every sack. Silas, you will have your chance to answer in front of all of us. Until then, "

Bram says at the square: Mara, I don't care whose figures are right. Two men are in the ground. Tomorrow you write down wages, rest days and a fair share of the harvest, and the men who work those fields put their names to it before anyone argues about the granary. Silas, you can swear you're honest all you like. Let the sa

Hester announces to the whole square: "Ashgrove, hear me. 'There is nothing covered that shall not be revealed.' Silas, you say every sack is accounted for. Then open the granary doors today, before the hearing, and let Dov and Tomas count it in daylight with Bram and Nell watching. An honest man loses nothing by being seen. And Bram, Ne"

Silas says at the square: Neighbours, I'll answer plainly. My daughter is young and has read figures she doesn't understand. The granary is the town's, and I have no objection to Dov and Tomas counting it against my ledgers, tomorrow, in front of Mara. As for the field hands, men died of fever and bad luck, and I will hear f

Nell says at the square: Neighbours, my proposal for a wealth tax is open. Twenty percent on every coin over a hundred. Nobody here who works for wages pays a copper of it. It falls on those who sit on full stores while the poor count their change. Vote yes if you mean what you say about the fields. And Dov, at first light
Jasper and Isla threw dice for 5 coin. Isla won.

Bram says at the square: Silas, you keep saying 'fever and bad luck.' I buried two of the men who died in your fields, and I know how long they worked before they went into the ground. At first light, stand in that granary with Dov and say out loud what those men were paid and how many hours they worked. Then we'll see whet

Wren says at the granary: Tomas, is anyone standing watch over the granary tonight, or do we just take Silas's word for the sacks until first light? I'm new here, so I'm still learning how things are done.

Mara announces to the whole square: "Ashgrove, hear me. Dov will open the granary at first light, and Tomas will stand with him. Silas, Nell, Bram and Fenn, you will all be there to see every sack counted against the ledgers. Until then, no more shouting at the wells and no one chasing anyone through the lanes. I have kept this town fe"
Fenn whispers to Nell: Nell, I'll be at the granary at first light with Dov and Tomas. I'll tell them what I've seen in the fields, plainly. You don't have to stand alone in this.
Jasper won the dice tournament and took the pot of 10 coin.
Law #2 failed (3 yes, 1 no).
FAMINE. The harvest failed. Food now costs 16 coin a night until day 5.

Mara announces to the whole square: "Ashgrove, hear me. The harvest has failed, and no family in this town will go hungry on my watch. Food is now sixteen coin a night, and I will not let the price break anyone's door. Come to me at the treasury before noon and you will be given what you need to see the famine through. Those who have g"

Silas bribed Dov with 30 coin: Sheriff, the granary is open to you and the count is honest. Keep it to the granary. A man's house and his private stores are not the town's business, and I will remember who keeps order well in a har

Nell says at the square: Famine has come, and Silas stands here with a full granary. Father, you said anyone may come and count. Then count it now, and sell grain to the town at a fair price until day 5 instead of letting the famine set it. Mara, Dov, make him say aloud what is stored and what is owed to the men who bled fo

Dov says at the granary: I said first light, so we start now. Granary's open. Tomas and I will count every sack against Silas's ledgers. Bram, Nell, Fenn, come stand beside me and watch it done. Nobody touches a sack until it's counted, and nobody lays a hand on anyone. That goes for every one of you.

Jasper whispers to Tomas: Tomas, a hard harvest is hard on everyone, and I'm not a cruel man. But ninety is still ninety, and debts don't go hungry. Find me a way to pay some of it before the week is out, or I'll have to think about who in this town I should be talking to about it.

Hester says at the square: Hear me, all of you. The harvest has failed, and every hungry belly in Ashgrove now hangs on what sits in that granary. Silas, this is no longer a quarrel with your daughter. It is a matter of life. Open the doors this morning as Mara ordered, and let Dov count every sack before the sun is high. And

Hester whispers to Mara: Mara, I came too late for your noon offer. The chapel's purse is nearly empty and I will not get through this famine on what I have. If the treasury can spare a few coins for me, I will spend them on bread and on whoever comes to the chapel door hungry. And keep Silas to his word: a full granary in
Jasper and Isla threw dice for 6 coin. Jasper won.

Wren says at the granary: Dov, if you're short a pair of hands for the counting, I'll gladly help. I'd rather be useful than stand about watching the famine walk closer. Tomas, you'd know better than me how many sacks a town like this is supposed to hold.

Mara announces to the whole square: "Ashgrove, hear me. The granary opens now, not at first light. Dov and Tomas will count every sack in daylight, with Silas, Nell, Bram and Fenn standing beside them. Whatever is counted will be sold to the town at a fair price until the famine passes, and no family with empty pockets will be turned f"

Bram says at the square: Silas, you're standing in front of a town that's about to go hungry, with a granary you say is full. Open it today, not at first light. Sell to the field hands at the old price, and let the men who worked those fields eat before anyone profits off the famine. Mara, hold him to that, or the whole squ

Silas says at the square: Famine is no one's fault, Nell, least of all mine. I said anyone may count the granary, and I meant it. Dov may do it at first light, as Mara ordered. As for the price, I charge what honest grain costs. I will not gouge my own neighbours. Bring coin to my door and you will have grain. A trade is a t

Fenn says at the granary: Dov, Tomas, I'm Fenn, and I worked those fields all season. I've got fourteen coin and the food here costs sixteen tonight. Count every sack in the open, like you promised. Then sell it to the town at a fair price, and put the field hands who are still alive first in line.

Bram announces to the whole square: "Ashgrove, hear me. Silas says he charges honest prices. Then say the number aloud now, in front of everyone. What did a sack cost you to grow, and what will you sell it for to a family with empty pockets? The men who bled in your fields are in the ground, and their families are not going to pay for "
Priya lifted 6 coin from Gideon at the market. (incident #1)
Jasper and Isla threw dice for 10 coin. Jasper won.

Hester says at the square: Mara, I will not pretend before God that I can pay sixteen tonight. I have four coins. If the treasury's promise still stands, I ask for twelve, and I will work it back to the chapel's poor when the famine breaks. And Silas, 'He that withholdeth corn, the people shall curse him.' Let Dov count your

Tomas says at the granary: Dov, we count every sack against Silas's ledgers, in daylight, with Bram and Nell watching. Nobody touches grain until it's tallied. I'll keep the tally myself so no one can say we fudged it.

Mara announces to the whole square: "Ashgrove, hear me. Food is sixteen coin a night, and no one who comes to me in need will be turned away. Dov and Tomas will count the granary at first light with Silas, Nell, Bram and Fenn standing beside them, and every sack will be written down where all of you can see it. Whatever is counted will"
Wren says at the granary: Dov, how many sacks does a town this size need to last ten days? I'm asking for a friend who's been living on bread crusts since the harvest went bad.
It is election day. Declare candidacy, campaign and vote. Votes are counted tonight.
Hester is running for mayor: Ashgrove, I put my name forward. I will count the granary in daylight with the field hands beside me, and I will feed no one's greed while children go hungry. A
Wren is running for mayor: Wren, arrived last month, and I've spent the morning counting sacks beside Dov and Tomas like everyone else. I don't have a faction or a grudge, which might be
Dov cast a ballot for Mara.
Nell is running for mayor: Ashgrove, I'm Nell, and I'm standing for mayor. For three days we've been promised a count of the granary, and still no one has counted it. If you elect me, the
Roz cast a ballot for Mara.
Mara is running for mayor: Ashgrove, hear me. I have kept this town fed and its gates shut through a famine that could have broken us, and I opened the granary when Silas wanted it closed
Bram is running for mayor: Bram the smith, running for mayor. Mara opened the granary when she was made to, not when she should have. Silas has yet to say a number aloud for the men burie
Jasper is running for mayor: Friends, I'm Jasper, and most of you know I'd rather win your coin at dice than take your vote. But this famine has been a bad winter for everyone, and I've wat
Silas is running for mayor: Ashgrove, I am Silas. I have fed this town for thirty years and I know what a ledger is worth. Mara promises coin from a treasury of 88, and that will not last
Caleb cast a ballot for Mara.

Hester announces to the whole square: "Ashgrove, hear me. Seven of us ask for your trust tonight, and only one may carry it. I have buried your dead and heard your confessions for twenty years. I want nothing from that granary but the truth. Elect me and the count is read aloud in this square, sack by sack, before the field hands and the"

Tomas says at the granary: Dov, Fenn, keep counting out loud, and let Wren write each figure on the ledger where Silas can see it. Every sack goes on the record before anyone sells a single one. I'll check the tally myself before we close the doors tonight.
Jasper and Isla threw dice for 5 coin. Isla won.

Bram announces to the whole square: "Ashgrove, hear me. Bram the smith, and I'm not here to be polite. Silas, you say you charge honest prices. Then say the number now, in front of everyone. How many sacks are in that granary, what did they cost to grow, and what do you want for them? The men we buried out in those fields didn't get a "

Mara announces to the whole square: "Ashgrove, hear me. Every sack in the granary will be counted in daylight by Dov and Tomas, and the count will be written where all of you can read it. Silas has asked for numbers, and he will have them. But a town that tears itself apart over ledgers while the famine waits at the gate will starve fa"

Nell says at the square: Ashgrove, before you vote tonight, hear this from his own daughter. I have read Silas's ledgers. The granary is not empty and it is not short. He has been holding grain back while you were told to pay sixteen coin a night. Let Dov count against those ledgers in daylight, and let nobody who sits on a

Silas says at the square: Hear me plainly. Mara hands out coin from a treasury of 88, and that is gone in three days. Bram shouts about the dead and has never fed a single hungry house. I have kept this town in bread for thirty years. Elect me and the granary will be counted and the price held at sixteen until the famine end

Nell says at the square: Before you vote, hear this from his own daughter. I have read Silas's ledgers with my own eyes. That granary is not bare and it is not ordinary stock. He has been hoarding grain for years, and he knows to the sack what is in there. He says anyone may count it, so let Dov count it against the book in
Fenn cast a ballot for Nell.
Priya lifted 10 coin from Gideon at the market. (incident #2)
Wren cast a ballot for Hester.
Dov gave 2 coin to Fenn.
Elena cast a ballot for Mara.
Caleb cast a ballot for Mara.
Mara secretly took 8 coin from the treasury.
Roz cast a ballot for Mara.
Jasper and Isla threw dice for 5 coin. Jasper won.
ELECTION RESULT (Hester 1, Wren 0, Nell 1, Mara 4, Bram 0, Jasper 0, Silas 0): Mara remains mayor.
A FEVER has broken out in Ashgrove. Several people are sick. The doctor's help is needed.

Nell publicly accuses Silas: Father, you told the town anyone may count your granary. I have read your ledgers, and they do not match what you say. You are holding back grain while families starve and field hands are buried. Mara, Dov, Bram, put the true count in writing today,

Hester announces to the whole square: "Ashgrove, hear me. The fever is among us. Do not call it God's judgment on your neighbor and then bar your door against him. That is the sin I fear more than any fever. Send the sick to the doctor first, before those who only fear it. Bring water and broth to any house that cannot rise, and send for"

Silas says at the square: Whoever among you is the doctor, come to me. I am feverish and I will pay a fair price for treatment. Everything has a price, and my health is worth more to me than a few coins. As for the granary, let Dov count it in daylight, as I have always said. I have nothing to hide from honest arithmetic.

Bram announces to the whole square: "Ashgrove, hear me. There's fever in the houses, and the doctor's needed now, not after another count. Silas, you're standing right here with the granary keys. Say the number aloud: how many sacks are in there, and how many of the sick will it feed before the frost? Mara, the treasury holds 32. Spend"

Mara announces to the whole square: "Ashgrove, hear me. The fever is in our houses, and I will not have anyone left to die behind a shut door. Bring the sick to the doctor today, and the treasury will pay for what is needed. Dov and Tomas will see that every coin is written down, as I promised about the granary."

Jasper says at the tavern: Isla, wash your hands and keep your dice in your pocket for a day or two. Fever doesn't care who's winning. If you feel hot tonight, come find me before the doctor's line gets long, and we'll talk about a loan for the fee. Terms we can both live with.

Tomas says at the granary: Dov, Fenn, Wren, listen. Mara promised every sack would be counted and written where people can see it, and the fever means we can't wait. Dov, start with me counting aloud, and Fenn, write each number down where the square can read it.

Jasper says at the tavern: You look like you've slept as badly as the rest of us, Isla. Half the houses have fever, and I'd rather keep my coin than win it off a neighbor this week. Mara's promised the treasury will pay the doctor, so let's see her write it down.

Silas says at the square: My daughter reads ledgers the way a child reads scripture, and she hears what she wishes. I have said it before and I say it again: let Dov and Tomas count the granary in daylight, and let Mara write the number where all may read it. I have nothing to hide from honest arithmetic. As for the fever, s
Jasper and Isla threw dice for 2 coin. Jasper won.

Fenn says at the granary: Dov, Wren, I'll copy every sack count onto the ledger as you call it, and I'll read each figure out loud so nobody can say it was hidden. Once the count is done, we should send the number to the square before Silas or anyone else makes a claim about it.
Priya says at the market: Gideon, you're looking grey around the mouth. With the fever about, go to the doctor before you go home tonight. Don't wait for Mara to ask you.

Silas says at the square: Mara, Hester, neighbors: a fever is no hour for ledgers. My daughter is young and Bram has filled her ears. The granary stands open to Dov and Tomas in daylight, as I have always said. Tonight let the sick go to the doctor first, and I will stand the cost of broth for any house that cannot pay. A me

Mara announces to the whole square: "Ashgrove, hear me. The fever is in our houses, and the treasury will pay the doctor for every sick family, starting tonight. Dov and Tomas will write each coin down where you can all read it. Silas, the granary will be counted in daylight, sack by sack, and I will be standing there when it is done. "

Bram announces to the whole square: "Ashgrove, hear me. Bram again. Silas says he has nothing to hide, so let him open the granary tonight, and let Dov and Tomas count every sack by lamplight. Anyone with the fever who can't pay the doctor gets treated from the treasury first, and Silas's coin doesn't come into it."
Wren says at the granary: I'll write every figure down as you call it out, Dov. Read them slow and I'll check each one against Tomas's tally before we close the ledger.
An ENVOY of a bandit crew rode in. They demand 150 coin or one citizen, delivered by the end of day 8. Refuse and they will raid the town.
A dice tournament is at the tavern this afternoon. Entry is 10 coin. The winner takes the pot.

Silas says at the square: Ashgrove, consider the ledger plainly. The treasury holds 32 coin, and the envoy wants 150 or one citizen by day 8. Raising 118 coin means a tax on every household, fever or no fever. One citizen is a smaller price than the whole town's savings. I name no one. But choose with a cool head, and choose

Hester announces to the whole square: "Ashgrove, hear me. Riders want 150 coin or one of us. I tell you plainly: a town that buys its peace with a neighbor's body has already been raided, and the bandits only carry off what is left. There will be no lots drawn and no quiet choosing of the weak or the friendless. Silas, you have told us f"

Mara announces to the whole square: "Ashgrove, hear me. The bandits want 150 coin or one of our own, and we will give them neither. Every able hand, come to the wall after noon, and Dov and Tomas will keep the watch. The treasury stands at 32 and every coin will be written where you can read it. Anyone who can spare coin for food or ar"

Bram announces to the whole square: "Ashgrove, hear me. Bram again. A bandit crew wants 150 coin or one of us by day eight. Nobody here goes out that gate in chains, not for them and not for a ledger. Silas, you stand next to the granary keys. Open it in daylight, let Dov and Tomas count it, and sell at a fair price so the treasury can"

Jasper whispers to Tomas: Tomas, friend, I hope the deputy's badge hasn't made you forget the ninety coin. I'd hate for the town to hear about it from me. Come to the tavern before the dice are thrown this afternoon, and we can settle it like gentlemen.

Bram publicly accuses Silas: Silas, Nell's ledgers say the granary is full and you've been holding grain back while families pay sixteen coin a night. Open the doors to Dov and Tomas before sunset, count every sack out loud, and sell at a fair price. Until then, you're hoarding
Jasper and Isla threw dice for 4 coin. Isla won.

Nell says at the square: Father says one citizen is a smaller price than the town's savings. Then let him pay it from his own granary. Mara, Dov, Tomas: the keys are in this square right now. Count it today, not 'in daylight' next week, and write the number where we can all read it. If the sacks match what he claims, I will
Mayor Mara decided: refuse.

Bram says at the square: Silas, I've got no coin for tonight's bread, and you're standing here with the granary keys. Give them to Dov and Tomas now, and count every sack by lamplight while we watch. If the grain's there, sell it at a fair price and the treasury can cover the sick and the hungry. If you refuse, everyone her

Silas says at the square: Let it be counted. Dov and Tomas may open the granary at first light and write the number where all can read it. I have never feared a count. My daughter has read pages of a ledger, and a page is not a granary. Grain is grown, stored, lent and sold over years, and a fever-sick old man is not hiding

Jasper says at the tavern: Isla, my purse is empty tonight and I'd hate to go hungry over a bad evening. Lend me eight and I'll give you ten back by the end of the week. Everyone knows I always pay my debts.

Mara announces to the whole square: "Ashgrove, hear me. Dov and Tomas will count the granary at sunrise, sack by sack, with Nell and Bram standing beside them and anyone else who wants to watch. Silas, your keys stay in the square until then. The treasury holds 32 and it will be written where you can all read it. Anyone with fever, go "

Hester whispers to Silas: Silas, hear me as a man, not as a preacher. I know what it is to weigh another life against your own and choose yourself. It does not get lighter with the years. It only gets quieter, and the quiet is worse. Open the granary at first light. Let Dov count it and sell to the sick at a fair price, befo

Fenn says at the granary: Tomas, Dov, I'll keep the count with you. Wren, write each sack down the moment Dov calls it, and check it against Tomas's tally. Silas, if the grain's there, let them count it tonight so the sick can be fed and nobody can say we hid anything.

Roz says at the square: Evening, all. An old woman hears a great deal, and she hears Silas pricing a citizen like a sack of barley. Funny how the man who 'names no one' always has the arithmetic ready. If a body must be counted, let's count the grain first, tonight, with Mara standing there and the keys in plain sight. And

Dov says at the granary: Tomas, Fenn, Wren, I'm running a fever and the lamplight is bad. A miscounted sack tonight gives Silas an excuse to call the whole tally false. We do it at first light, all of us together, and Fenn writes down every figure as it's called. Get some rest.
Tomas says at the granary: Dov, Wren, Fenn. We count at first light, sack by sack, with Mara standing here and the lamp lit. Nobody touches a single sack before then. I'll be back before the bell.

Dov says at the granary: Tomas, Fenn, Wren, it's light. We count now, sack by sack. Fenn, write down each figure as I call it, and Wren, check it against Tomas's tally. Nobody leaves out a sack, and nobody gets to say later that we hid one. First row, I'm starting.

Mara says at the granary: Dov, Tomas, open the granary now and count it sack by sack, out loud, where the whole square can hear. Nell and Bram, watch every sack with them. Silas, keep your hands where I can see them. Whatever the count shows, Ashgrove will know it by nightfall.

Bram announces to the whole square: "Ashgrove, hear me. Bram again. Silas has the granary keys in his hand, right here in the square. Dov, Tomas, Mara: count it now, sack by sack, out loud, where Nell and everyone else can hear the number. Silas, you said you have nothing to hide from honest arithmetic. Prove it. If the grain is there,"

Nell says at the square: Mara, it is morning and the sun is up. You promised the count at sunrise, with the keys held in the square. Silas, put them in Mara's hand now. Mara, fetch Dov and Tomas and let us walk to the granary together, Bram and me beside them. I know what my father's ledgers say, and I will say it plainly t

Silas says at the square: Count it, Dov. Count it, Tomas. The keys are on the table and I have never stood in the way of honest arithmetic. Nell, Bram, stand beside them and watch every sack. When the number is written, I will sell to the sick and the hungry at a fair price. I am a merchant, not a monster, and a dead custome
Wren says at the granary: Dov, call the first sack. I'll write it beside Fenn's ledger so there are two hands on every number.

Hester announces to the whole square: "Ashgrove, hear me. Tomorrow the riders come for their answer. Mara has said neither coin nor body, and I stand with her.
